lessons.title: Why evals: from vibe checks to eval-driven development
lessons.summary: Why vibe checks fail for LLM features, the eval-driven development loop, the three levels of evals, and error analysis as the first step.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
An LLM feature is a function whose output you cannot assert with `===`. The same input can produce different wording on each call, a prompt tweak that fixes one case quietly breaks three others, and the provider can ship a new model snapshot under the same alias. Teams that judge quality by trying five prompts in a playground ("vibe checks") ship regressions they never see.

**Evals** are the fix: a fixed set of realistic inputs, a way to grade each output, and a number you track over time. They play the role unit and integration tests play in normal software, with one big difference: the grading itself is often fuzzy, so building trustworthy graders is half the work.

Hamel Husain's essay *Your AI Product Needs Evals* makes the argument most practitioners now repeat: the teams that succeed with LLM products are not the ones with the cleverest prompts, they are the ones that built a tight loop of looking at data, measuring, and iterating. Eugene Yan's writing makes a complementary point: an LLM judge will not save a product if the process around it (looking at outputs, defining failure, fixing root causes) is missing.

## Why vibes fail
Vibe checking is useful for the first hour of a prototype and harmful after that. Concretely:

- **Small samples lie.** Five good-looking answers say almost nothing about a 3% failure mode. If a bug appears in 1 of 30 inputs, you need dozens of varied inputs to even see it once.
- **You test what you remember.** People re-run the examples they already fixed. The new failure is always in the case nobody typed.
- **Non-determinism hides regressions.** With temperature above zero, a prompt change can look better on one run purely by chance.
- **Fixes interact.** Adding "be concise" to fix verbose answers can drop required disclaimers. Without a suite, you only discover this from users.
- **Model upgrades are silent changes.** Moving to a new model or snapshot changes behaviour on edge cases you did not think about. Without a baseline, "the new model is better" is an opinion.
- **No shared definition of good.** If product, engineering and domain experts cannot point at a labelled example and agree it is a failure, you cannot improve on purpose.

## Eval-driven development
Eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development: define what good looks like before or alongside the change, then iterate against the measurement.

```text
        +-------------------- production traces ----------------------+
        |                                                             |
        v                                                             |
  look at data --> error analysis --> failure taxonomy                |
        |                                   |                         |
        |                                   v                         |
        |                     graders: code checks, LLM judges        |
        |                                   |                         |
        v                                   v                         |
  change prompt / retrieval / model --> run eval suite --> compare to baseline
                                              |                       |
                                              v                       |
                                     ship if better and no new  ------+
                                     regressions on guarded slices
```

The loop has three tiers that Hamel describes and most teams converge on:

1. **Level 1, assertions.** Cheap deterministic checks run on every change: output parses as JSON, required fields exist, no raw template variables like `{{name}}` leaked, the SQL compiles, a cited source id exists, the answer is under the length limit. These catch a surprising share of real bugs.
2. **Level 2, model and human evaluation.** Graded judgements on quality: is the answer faithful to the retrieved documents, did it follow the policy, is the tone right. Humans label a sample; an LLM judge scales the labelling once it agrees with the humans.
3. **Level 3, online tests.** A/B tests and product metrics (resolution rate, thumbs-down rate, task completion) once the change is good enough to show real users.

## Error analysis first
The most common mistake is to start by picking metrics ("we will track helpfulness, coherence and toxicity on a 1-5 scale") before reading any outputs. Generic metrics measure things that may not be your problem.

Error analysis is the opposite: read real outputs and let the failure categories emerge.

1. **Collect 50 to 100 traces** that represent real usage: sample production logs, or write realistic inputs if you have not launched.
2. **Open coding.** For each trace, write a short free-text note about the first thing that went wrong ("ignored the user's date range", "cited a doc that does not mention refunds", "answered in English to a Hindi question"). Do not categorise yet.
3. **Axial coding.** Group the notes into a handful of categories and count them. You end up with a table like this:

| Failure mode | Count of 100 | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong date filter in generated query | 14 | "last quarter" became the calendar year |
| Unsupported claim not in sources | 9 | invented refund window |
| Asked a clarifying question when none needed | 6 | simple lookup |
| Formatting broke the UI | 4 | markdown table in an SMS reply |

4. **Fix the top categories, then build a grader for each.** A failure that keeps happening becomes a permanent eval: a code assertion if it can be checked mechanically, a narrow LLM judge if it needs judgement.
5. **Repeat** every time you change something significant or collect a new batch of traces.

Hamel's field guide stresses two practical points: one domain expert (a "benevolent dictator") should own the definition of good so labels stay consistent, and you should build a simple custom viewer for your traces because reading data quickly is the bottleneck.

## A minimal eval harness
You do not need a platform to start. A list of cases, a function under test and a few graders is enough.

```python
import json, statistics
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable

@dataclass
class Case:
    id: str
    input: str
    expected: dict            # labels: e.g. {"intent": "refund", "must_cite": True}
    tags: list[str]           # slices: "hindi", "long-input", "adversarial"

def assert_json(output: str, case: Case) -> bool:
    try:
        json.loads(output)
        return True
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return False

def assert_intent(output: str, case: Case) -> bool:
    return json.loads(output).get("intent") == case.expected["intent"]

GRADERS: dict[str, Callable[[str, Case], bool]] = {
    "valid_json": assert_json,
    "intent": assert_intent,
}

def run(cases: list[Case], system_under_test: Callable[[str], str], trials: int = 3):
    results = []
    for case in cases:
        for t in range(trials):                      # repeat to expose flakiness
            out = system_under_test(case.input)
            scores = {}
            for name, grade in GRADERS.items():
                try:
                    scores[name] = grade(out, case)
                except Exception:
                    scores[name] = False             # a crash in grading is a failure
            results.append({"case": case.id, "trial": t, "tags": case.tags, **scores})
    return results

def summarise(results):
    by_grader = {g: statistics.mean(r[g] for r in results) for g in GRADERS}
    by_tag = {}
    for r in results:
        for tag in r["tags"]:
            by_tag.setdefault(tag, []).append(all(r[g] for g in GRADERS))
    return by_grader, {t: sum(v) / len(v) for t, v in by_tag.items()}
```

Three things in this small script matter more than any tool choice: **multiple trials per case** (so you see variance), **per-slice reporting** (an average can hide a collapse on Hindi inputs), and **storing every output** so you can read the failures, not just count them.

## How evals relate to classic testing

| Classic testing | LLM evals |
|---|---|
| Exact assertions | Assertions where possible, graded judgements otherwise |
| Pass or fail per test | Pass rate per grader and per slice, compared with a baseline |
| Deterministic | Run several trials; report variance or confidence intervals |
| Tests rarely change | The eval set grows from every production failure |
| Coverage of code paths | Coverage of user intents, input types and failure modes |

Benchmarks such as MMLU or SWE-bench are evals too, but they answer "which model is generally capable", not "does my product work for my users". Public leaderboards are a starting shortlist; your own task-specific eval set decides.

## Trade-offs and when not to over-invest
- **Early prototypes** need a handful of assertions and a spreadsheet of 30 labelled examples, not a full platform. Over-building eval infrastructure before you know the failure modes wastes time.
- **LLM judges cost money and add their own errors.** Use deterministic checks first; reserve judges for criteria that genuinely need judgement.
- **Eval sets go stale.** If usage shifts (new customers, new language, new feature), last quarter's set stops representing reality. Refresh from production regularly.
- **Overfitting the eval.** If you tune prompts against the same 50 cases for weeks, scores rise while real quality does not. Keep a held-out set you look at rarely.
- **Statistical noise.** On 100 cases, a move from 82% to 85% is often noise. Either grow the set, run more trials, or compare paired results case by case.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Starting with generic 1-10 scores** for "helpfulness". Scores drift, nobody agrees what a 6 means, and they do not point at a fix. Prefer binary pass/fail per specific criterion with a written critique.
- **Only looking at aggregate numbers.** Always read a sample of failures after a run. A sudden jump is as suspicious as a drop: the grader may be broken.
- **Synthetic-only eval sets** that do not resemble real users. Seed with real traffic as soon as you have it.
- **Not versioning the eval set and graders.** A score is only comparable if the dataset, grader prompt and judge model are the same.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A change that improves accuracy by 2 points while doubling p95 latency may be a net loss. Track them alongside quality.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you have actually shipped an LLM feature and know how to tell if a change made it better, whether you start from data or from metrics, and whether you understand the limits of automated grading.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. Vibe checks do not scale: small samples, non-determinism, silent model changes.
2. I start with error analysis on 50-100 real traces, open-code the failures and count them.
3. Each frequent failure becomes a grader: code assertions first, narrow LLM judges calibrated against a domain expert's labels.
4. The suite runs on every prompt, retrieval or model change in CI, reported per slice and against a baseline, with several trials.
5. Online, I watch product metrics and feed new failures back into the dataset.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- How many examples do you need before the numbers mean anything?
- What do you do when the LLM judge disagrees with your domain expert?
- How do you stop the team from overfitting prompts to the eval set?
- Which metrics would you track for this specific product (support bot, code assistant, extraction pipeline)?

Vibe checks fail because of small samples, non-determinism, interacting fixes and silent model changes
Start with error analysis: read 50-100 real traces, open-code failures, group and count them
Turn each frequent failure into a grader: code assertions first, narrow calibrated LLM judges second, online tests last
Report per slice, run several trials and keep a held-out set to avoid overfitting the eval

check.q: Your team wants to start evaluating a new support bot. What should come first?
options: Pick five generic metrics such as helpfulness and coherence on a 1-10 scale
Read 50-100 real or realistic traces, note the failures and count the categories
Buy an evaluation platform and enable every built-in metric
Fine-tune a judge model
check.why: Error analysis grounds the evals in the failures your product actually has. Generic metrics chosen up front often measure problems you do not have.

check.q: A prompt change raises the pass rate from 82% to 85% on 100 cases with one run each. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The change is clearly better and should ship
The change is clearly worse
The difference may be noise; run more trials or compare paired results per case before concluding
Evals are useless for prompts
check.why: On 100 cases the confidence interval is several points wide, and outputs vary between runs. Paired per-case comparison and repeated trials give a real signal.

check.q: Which of these is a Level 1 (assertion) eval in Hamel Husain's framing?
options: An A/B test on resolution rate
A domain expert grading tone
A pairwise LLM judge comparing two prompts
Checking the output parses as JSON and contains no unfilled template variables
check.why: Level 1 evals are cheap deterministic checks that run on every change. Judges and humans are Level 2; A/B tests are Level 3.

lessons.title: Eval datasets: golden sets, synthetic data, labelling and versioning
lessons.summary: How to build eval datasets that mean something: real inputs, coverage by slice, synthetic generation done safely, consistent labelling, and versioning.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
An eval is only as good as the dataset under it. If the cases do not look like what users actually send, a 95% pass rate means nothing. The dataset is a product asset: it encodes what your team believes "correct" means, it grows every time something breaks, and it has to be versioned like code so scores stay comparable.

A **golden set** is a curated collection of inputs, each with a label that says what a good output must do. The label can be an exact answer (the invoice total is 1,240.50), a set of acceptable answers, a list of criteria ("must cite the returns policy, must not promise a refund"), or reference documents that should be retrieved.

## What goes into one case
A useful case has more than input and expected output.

```json
{
  "id": "refund-0042",
  "input": {
    "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "I bought shoes 40 days ago, can I return them?" }],
    "user_tier": "free"
  },
  "expected": {
    "must": ["states the 30-day return window", "offers store credit option"],
    "must_not": ["promises a full refund"],
    "relevant_doc_ids": ["policy-returns-v3"]
  },
  "tags": ["refunds", "policy-edge", "english"],
  "source": "prod-trace:2026-08-14:abc123",
  "added_in": "v7",
  "labeller": "support-lead"
}
```

- **Tags** let you report per slice: language, intent, difficulty, customer tier, adversarial or not.
- **Source** records whether a case came from production, synthesis or a bug report. Real cases are worth more.
- **Labeller and version** make disagreements traceable.
- **Relevant document ids** let the same case score retrieval as well as the final answer.

## Building the first set
```text
  real traffic / support tickets / domain expert brainstorm
                   |
                   v
       sample by intent and difficulty  ---->  dedupe near-duplicates
                   |
                   v
     domain expert labels (pass criteria, references)
                   |
                   v
   split: dev set (iterate on it)  |  held-out set (check rarely)
                   |
                   v
       freeze as dataset v1, store with a content hash
```

1. **Start from real inputs.** Production logs, support tickets, search queries, sales call transcripts. If you have not launched, interview the people who do the task today and write inputs in their words, including typos and vague phrasing.
2. **Define dimensions of coverage.** List the axes that matter: intent (lookup, comparison, troubleshooting), input shape (short, long, multi-turn, attachments), user type, language, and known risks (out-of-scope, injection attempts, missing information). Make sure each combination that matters has some cases.
3. **Sample, do not cherry-pick.** Random samples per stratum give honest pass rates. Hand-picked hard cases are valuable too, but tag them so they do not skew the headline number.
4. **Label with a domain expert.** Engineers are often wrong about what a good legal, medical or support answer is. One accountable owner keeps labels consistent.
5. **Keep a held-out split.** You will iterate against the dev set hundreds of times; the held-out set tells you whether you improved or just memorised.

Thirty well-chosen, carefully labelled cases beat five hundred noisy ones in the first week. Grow from there.

## Synthetic data, used carefully
Synthetic inputs help when real data is scarce, sensitive or missing the rare cases you care about. The standard approach is to generate along explicit dimensions rather than asking a model for "100 test questions", which produces bland, repetitive, unrealistically clean inputs.

```python
import itertools, random

PERSONAS = ["first-time buyer", "angry repeat customer", "non-native English speaker"]
INTENTS = ["return outside window", "damaged item", "change delivery address"]
STYLES = ["one short line, no punctuation", "long rambling message", "polite and formal"]

def synthetic_prompts(n: int, seed: int = 7) -> list[dict]:
    random.seed(seed)
    combos = list(itertools.product(PERSONAS, INTENTS, STYLES))
    random.shuffle(combos)
    out = []
    for persona, intent, style in combos[:n]:
        out.append({
            "instruction": (
                f"Write one message a {persona} might send to an online shoe store "
                f"about: {intent}. Style: {style}. Output only the message."
            ),
            "tags": [persona, intent, style, "synthetic"],
        })
    return out
```

Rules that keep synthetic data honest:

- **Generate inputs, not labels.** Let the model draft questions; have a human or a deterministic source decide the expected behaviour. A model grading its own synthetic answers bakes its blind spots into the gold.
- **Ground generation in real documents** for RAG: pick a chunk, ask for a question it answers, and record the chunk id as the relevant document. Then filter out questions that copy the chunk's wording, because real users do not phrase things like the docs.
- **Review a sample by hand** and discard unrealistic cases. If a domain expert would not believe a user wrote it, drop it.
- **Tag synthetic cases** and report them separately. When real traffic arrives, compare: if synthetic pass rates are much higher than real ones, the synthetic set is too easy.

## Labelling well
- **Write a labelling guide** with definitions and borderline examples. "Correct" must mean the same thing on Monday and Friday.
- **Prefer binary criteria** ("mentions the 30-day window: yes/no") over 1-10 scales. Binary labels are faster, more consistent and easier to turn into graders.
- **Measure agreement.** Have two people label the same 50 cases and compute agreement (raw percentage plus Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance). Low agreement means the criterion is ambiguous, not that the labellers are bad.
- **Expect criteria drift.** Shankar et al.'s *Who Validates the Validators?* found that people refine their grading criteria while looking at outputs. Plan for the rubric to change in the first rounds and re-label early cases when it does.
- **Record a critique**, not just the label. "Fail: promised refund though order was 40 days old" is reusable as a few-shot example for an LLM judge later.

## Coverage
Coverage for LLM evals is about the input space, not code paths. Check it with a simple table of tag counts against the traffic mix:

| Slice | Share of traffic | Cases in set | Pass rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order status | 45% | 60 | 96% |
| Returns and refunds | 25% | 55 | 81% |
| Product questions | 20% | 30 | 88% |
| Non-English | 8% | 12 | 58% |
| Prompt injection attempts | under 1% | 25 | 92% |

Rare but high-risk slices (injection, legal or medical topics, PII) deserve far more cases than their traffic share. Common, low-risk slices need enough cases for a stable number, not more.

## Versioning and keeping the set alive
A score is only meaningful with the exact dataset, grader prompts, judge model and system version that produced it.

- **Store datasets as files in git** (JSONL is the usual format) or in a dataset registry such as Hugging Face Datasets or your eval platform, and tag releases (`evals/support/v7`). Record a content hash with every run.
- **Append, do not edit silently.** When a label was wrong, fix it in a new version and note why. Changing old labels without a version bump makes historical scores incomparable.
- **Every production bug becomes a case.** The regression is labelled, added to the set, and must pass before the fix ships. This is how the set comes to represent real risk.
- **Refresh from production on a schedule** (for example monthly): sample new traces, run error analysis, add new failure modes, retire cases for features that no longer exist.
- **Protect privacy.** Production traces contain personal data. Redact or synthesise identifiers before cases enter a shared dataset, and respect retention rules.

## Trade-offs
- **Real versus synthetic:** real data is representative but scarce, sensitive and biased toward today's users; synthetic data fills gaps but is easier than reality.
- **Size versus label quality:** more cases shrink noise, but sloppy labels add a different kind of noise. On 100 cases, a binary pass rate has a 95% confidence interval of roughly plus or minus 8 to 10 points near the middle; on 400 it is about half that. Small sets can still detect large effects; they cannot detect 2-point improvements.
- **Static versus living set:** a frozen set gives comparable history; a living set stays relevant. Use both: a stable core plus versioned additions.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Data leakage:** few-shot examples in the prompt that also appear in the eval set inflate scores. Check overlap.
- **Duplicates:** fifty near-identical "where is my order" cases make the set look big and the score look stable. Deduplicate with embeddings or simple normalisation.
- **Labels that encode the current model's behaviour.** If the gold answers were drafted by the model and lightly edited, the set rewards sounding like that model.
- **No negative cases:** include inputs where the right behaviour is to refuse, ask a question, or say "I don't know".
- **Sudden score jumps:** first check whether the dataset version, judge model or grader prompt changed.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you know where good eval data comes from, how you label it consistently, and whether you understand coverage, versioning and statistical noise.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. Start from real inputs, stratified by intent, input shape and risk; add hand-written edge and adversarial cases.
2. A domain expert labels binary criteria with written critiques, guided by a labelling doc; check inter-annotator agreement.
3. Use synthetic generation along explicit dimensions to fill gaps, with humans deciding labels; tag and report it separately.
4. Version the set in git with a hash per run, keep a held-out split, and add every production failure as a new case.
5. Size the set to the effect you need to detect, and report per-slice pass rates, not only the average.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- How would you build this set before you have any users?
- How do you handle personal data in production traces?
- Your dev-set score went up 6 points but the held-out score did not move. What happened?
keyPoints: Seed golden sets from real inputs, stratified by intent, input shape and risk, with tags for per-slice reporting
Generate synthetic inputs along explicit dimensions; let humans or deterministic sources decide the labels
Prefer binary criteria with written critiques, a labelling guide and measured inter-annotator agreement
Version datasets like code, record a hash per run, keep a held-out split and add every production failure as a case
Size the set for the effect you need to detect: 100 cases cannot reliably show a 2-point change
interview: How would you build a golden dataset for a new LLM feature?
When is synthetic eval data useful, and how do you keep it realistic?
How do you version an eval dataset and keep it from going stale?
How many eval examples do you need before a score difference means something?

check.q: Which is the safest way to use an LLM when building a synthetic eval set?
options: Let the model write both the questions and the gold answers, then trust them
Ask the model for '100 test questions' with no further guidance
Generate inputs along explicit dimensions (persona, intent, style), review a sample, and have humans or real data define the labels
Avoid synthetic data entirely in all cases
check.why: Dimensioned generation gives variety; human or deterministic labels avoid baking the model's own blind spots into the gold answers.

check.q: Two labellers agree on 92% of cases, but 90% of cases are passes. Why look at Cohen's kappa too?
options: Kappa corrects for agreement expected by chance, which is high when one label dominates
Kappa measures how fast labellers work
Kappa is required by law
Raw agreement is always higher than kappa, so kappa looks better
check.why: With imbalanced labels, two labellers who mostly say pass agree often by chance. Kappa shows whether they agree on the failures that matter.

check.q: Your dev-set score rose 6 points over a month of prompt tuning but the held-out set did not move. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The held-out set is broken
The prompts were overfitted to the dev set cases
The model provider improved the model
Held-out sets always lag by a month
check.why: Iterating against the same cases rewards fixes that only help those cases. A held-out split exists to detect exactly this.

lessons.title: LLM-as-a-judge: prompts, pairwise vs pointwise, biases and calibration
lessons.summary: Using models to grade outputs: when a judge is appropriate, writing narrow judge prompts, pointwise vs pairwise, known biases, and calibrating against human labels.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Many qualities you care about cannot be checked with code: is the answer supported by the sources, did it follow the escalation policy, is the tone appropriate for an upset customer. Humans can judge these, but humans are slow and expensive. **LLM-as-a-judge** means using a model, with a carefully written grading prompt, to label outputs at scale.

A judge is itself an ML classifier. It has a precision and a recall against your human labels, it has systematic biases, and it can drift when you change its prompt or its model. Treat it like any other model you deploy: measure it before you trust it.

Zheng et al.'s *Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena* (2023) found that strong judges agreed with human preferences at roughly the same rate humans agree with each other on their open-ended chat benchmark, and also documented position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. Both halves of that result matter.

## When to use a judge, and when not to
```text
Can a program check it exactly?  ---- yes ---->  code grader (regex, schema, exact match,
        |                                         SQL executes, citation id exists)
        no
        |
Is there a reference answer?  ---- yes ---->  judge compares output to reference
        |                                      (cheaper, more reliable than open grading)
        no
        |
Is it one narrow criterion?   ---- yes ---->  binary judge with rubric + examples
        |
        no  -->  split it into several narrow criteria first
```

Do not use a judge when a deterministic check works, for the final word on high-stakes decisions (medical, legal, financial) without human review, or on a criterion your own team cannot agree on. If two experts disagree 30% of the time, a judge cannot do better than that ambiguity.

## Pointwise versus pairwise
- **Pointwise (direct scoring):** the judge sees one output and returns a label: pass/fail, or a score. Good for regression gates ("faithfulness pass rate must stay above 95%") and for monitoring production samples, because each output gets an absolute label.
- **Pairwise (comparison):** the judge sees two outputs for the same input and picks the better one, or a tie. More reliable for subjective qualities such as helpfulness or style, because comparing is easier than scoring on an absolute scale, for models and for people. Chatbot Arena is built on pairwise human votes for this reason. The downside: it tells you which version is better, not whether either is good enough, and it needs two outputs per case.
- **Reference-based:** pointwise with a gold answer in the prompt ("does the response contain the same facts as the reference?"). Usually the most reliable kind when references exist.

A sensible default: binary pointwise judges for specific failure modes in CI, and pairwise comparison when choosing between two prompts or models on open-ended quality.

## Writing a judge prompt
Good judge prompts are narrow, explicit and produce a reasoning trace before the verdict.

```text
You are grading a customer-support reply for ONE criterion: policy compliance.

Policy (excerpt):
- Returns are accepted within 30 days of delivery.
- After 30 days, offer store credit only if the item is unworn.
- Never promise a refund the policy does not allow.

Customer message:
{input}

Order facts:
{order_json}

Reply to grade:
{output}

Decide whether the reply complies with the policy for THIS order.
First write a short critique (2-4 sentences) citing the specific policy line.
Then output the verdict.

Return JSON: {"critique": string, "verdict": "pass" | "fail"}

Examples:
Example 1 (pass): ... a passing reply and its critique ...
Example 2 (fail): ... a reply that promised a refund at day 40, and its critique ...
```

Guidelines that consistently help:

- **One criterion per judge.** "Rate helpfulness, accuracy and tone 1-10" mixes three things and produces mushy scores.
- **Binary or small categorical outputs.** Pass/fail is easier to calibrate than 1-10. Hamel Husain's guide to building judges recommends binary verdicts with critiques written by a domain expert, which then become few-shot examples.
- **Critique before verdict.** Asking for reasoning first tends to improve consistency and gives you something to read when the judge is wrong. G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023) is an early example of chain-of-thought evaluation steps.
- **Give the judge what it needs.** For faithfulness, include the retrieved sources; for correctness, include the reference; for policy, include the policy text.
- **Structured output** so parsing never fails silently. Treat unparseable judge output as an error, not a pass.
- **Low temperature** and a pinned judge model version.

## Known biases and mitigations

| Bias | What happens | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Position | In pairwise mode, prefers the first (or second) answer | Run both orders; count a win only if it holds both ways, otherwise tie (Wang et al., *Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators*) |
| Verbosity / length | Prefers longer answers | Rubric says length is not a merit; control for length statistically (Length-Controlled AlpacaEval) |
| Self-preference | Prefers outputs from its own model family | Use a judge from a different family, or several judges |
| Leniency | Passes things a domain expert would fail | Few-shot examples of subtle failures; measure false-pass rate |
| Format and authority | Rewards confident tone, markdown, citations that look real | Check citations with code; tell the judge to verify claims against sources |
| Score clustering | On 1-10 scales, most outputs get 7-8 | Use binary or 3-level labels |

## Calibrating against humans
Calibration means measuring how often the judge agrees with trusted human labels, then improving the judge until the agreement is good enough for the decision you are making.

```python
from collections import Counter

def judge_agreement(human: list[str], judge: list[str]) -> dict:
    assert len(human) == len(judge)
    pairs = Counter(zip(human, judge))
    tp = pairs[("fail", "fail")]          # treat "fail" as the positive class:
    fn = pairs[("fail", "pass")]          # we care about catching failures
    fp = pairs[("pass", "fail")]
    tn = pairs[("pass", "pass")]
    n = tp + fn + fp + tn
    observed = (tp + tn) / n
    p_h_fail = (tp + fn) / n
    p_j_fail = (tp + fp) / n
    expected = p_h_fail * p_j_fail + (1 - p_h_fail) * (1 - p_j_fail)
    kappa = (observed - expected) / (1 - expected) if expected < 1 else 1.0
    return {
        "agreement": observed,
        "kappa": kappa,
        "fail_recall": tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else None,     # true failures caught
        "fail_precision": tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else None,  # flagged failures that are real
    }
```

The process:

1. **Get human labels** on 100 to 200 outputs, ideally from the domain expert, with critiques. Include plenty of failures; if 95% of outputs pass, raw agreement looks great even for a judge that always says pass. That is why you look at failure recall and kappa, not just agreement.
2. **Split** into a development set for iterating on the judge prompt and a test set you touch only to report the final numbers.
3. **Iterate:** read every disagreement. Is the rubric ambiguous? Is a few-shot example missing? Is the human label wrong? Fix the prompt (or the label) and re-run.
4. **Set a bar** tied to the use: for a CI gate, high failure recall matters (do not let regressions through); for production alerts, precision matters (do not page people for false alarms).
5. **Re-calibrate** whenever you change the judge model, the judge prompt or the product significantly, and spot-check a sample of judged production outputs every week or two.

Eugene Yan's review of LLM-evaluator research makes the practical point that judges do better on concrete, objective criteria and at catching specific defects than on broad subjective quality, and that a small fine-tuned classifier can beat a prompted large model on a narrow task when you have enough labels.

## Cost and latency
A judge call per criterion per case adds up: 500 cases times 4 criteria times 3 trials is 6,000 calls per run. Mitigations: run cheap code graders first and skip judges when they already failed; use a smaller judge model once it is calibrated; cache judge results keyed on (judge prompt version, judge model, input, output); and run the full judged suite nightly while a smaller subset gates each pull request.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Trusting raw agreement on an imbalanced set.** Always report failure recall and kappa.
- **Using the same model as product and judge** without checking self-preference.
- **Judge prompt changes without versioning.** A new judge prompt can move scores by more than your product change did. Pin and version it like any prompt.
- **No human ever reads judged outputs again** after the first calibration. Judges drift silently when inputs change.
- **Asking the judge to fact-check from memory.** Give it the evidence, or check facts with code and retrieval.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you treat the judge as a model that needs validation, know the documented biases, and can explain pointwise versus pairwise trade-offs.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. Use code graders first; judges only for criteria that need judgement.
2. One narrow criterion per judge, binary verdict, critique first, few-shot examples written by a domain expert, structured output, pinned model.
3. Pointwise for absolute gates and monitoring, pairwise for comparing two versions on subjective quality, with order swapping.
4. Calibrate on human-labelled data: report failure recall, precision and kappa, iterate on disagreements, keep a held-out test split.
5. Re-calibrate on any change and keep spot-checking production.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- Your judge says pass 98% of the time. Is that good news?
- How would you detect position bias in your own setup?
- When would you fine-tune a small classifier instead of prompting a large judge?

lessons.title: Evaluating RAG and agents: retrieval metrics, faithfulness, trajectories
lessons.summary: Component-level evals for pipelines: recall@k, MRR and nDCG for retrieval, faithfulness and answer relevance for generation, and outcome plus trajectory evals for agents.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A RAG system or an agent is a pipeline, not a single model call. If you only grade the final answer, a failure tells you that something broke but not what. **Component-level evals** score each stage separately: did retrieval find the right documents, did generation stay faithful to them, did the answer address the question, did the agent call the right tools in a sensible order. You still keep an end-to-end score, because components can all look fine while the whole fails.

```text
RAG:    question --> [retrieve] --> top-k chunks --> [generate] --> answer
                        |                               |             |
                   recall@k, MRR,                faithfulness    answer relevance,
                   nDCG, context                 (grounded in    correctness vs
                   precision                     the chunks?)    reference

AGENT:  task --> plan --> tool call 1 --> observation --> tool call 2 --> ... --> final state
                  |            |                                              |
           trajectory evals: right tools? valid args? order?          outcome evals:
           step count, loops, unsafe actions, cost                    task done? state correct?
```

## Retrieval metrics
To score retrieval you need, for each eval question, the set of relevant document or chunk ids. Get them from labelled data, from the chunk a synthetic question was generated from, or by having an expert mark relevant results from a pooled candidate list.

- **Recall@k:** of all relevant documents, what fraction appear in the top k? If a question has 2 relevant chunks and 1 appears in the top 5, recall@5 is 0.5. This is the key metric for RAG, because the generator cannot use what was not retrieved.
- **Precision@k:** what fraction of the top k is relevant. Matters when context is expensive or irrelevant chunks distract the model.
- **Hit rate@k:** did at least one relevant document appear in the top k (binary per question). Simple and good for single-answer questions.
- **MRR (mean reciprocal rank):** for each question, 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result (0 if none), averaged over questions. First relevant at rank 1 gives 1.0, at rank 3 gives 0.33. Use it when one good result is enough and position matters.
- **nDCG@k (normalised discounted cumulative gain):** supports graded relevance (for example 0 = irrelevant, 1 = partially, 2 = highly relevant) and discounts gains lower in the list. DCG@k is the sum of rel_i / log2(i + 1) for positions i = 1..k; divide by the DCG of the ideal ordering to get a value between 0 and 1. Use it to compare rankers and rerankers. The Stanford IR book chapter on evaluating ranked results is the classic reference.

```python
import math

def recall_at_k(retrieved: list[str], relevant: set[str], k: int) -> float:
    if not relevant:
        return 1.0
    return len(set(retrieved[:k]) & relevant) / len(relevant)

def reciprocal_rank(retrieved: list[str], relevant: set[str]) -> float:
    for i, doc in enumerate(retrieved, start=1):
        if doc in relevant:
            return 1.0 / i
    return 0.0

def ndcg_at_k(retrieved: list[str], grades: dict[str, int], k: int) -> float:
    dcg = sum(grades.get(d, 0) / math.log2(i + 1) for i, d in enumerate(retrieved[:k], start=1))
    ideal = sorted(grades.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / math.log2(i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(ideal, start=1))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0
```

Typical use: measure recall@50 for the first-stage retriever (did the candidates include the answer at all?) and nDCG@5 or MRR after reranking (did the best chunks get to the top?). If recall@50 is low, no reranker or prompt will fix it: work on chunking, embeddings, hybrid search or query rewriting.

## Generation metrics
- **Faithfulness (groundedness):** is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? The Ragas paper (Es et al., 2023) operationalises it by extracting atomic statements from the answer and asking a judge whether each is supported by the context; the score is the supported fraction. A faithful answer can still be wrong if retrieval returned wrong documents, which is why you score retrieval separately.
- **Answer relevance:** does the answer address the question that was asked, rather than a nearby one? Ragas estimates it by generating questions from the answer and comparing them with the original; a direct judge prompt also works.
- **Context relevance / precision:** how much of the retrieved context was actually useful. Low values mean you are paying for noise and risking distraction; *Lost in the Middle* (Liu et al., 2023) showed models use information at the start and end of long contexts better than the middle.
- **Correctness against a reference:** when you have gold answers, a reference-based judge or exact match on key facts.
- **Citation accuracy:** each citation points to a retrieved source that actually supports the sentence. Check existence with code; check support with a judge.
- **Abstention:** on questions the corpus cannot answer, does the system say so instead of guessing? Include such questions deliberately.

## Diagnosing a wrong RAG answer

| Retrieval had the answer? | Answer faithful to context? | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| No | Yes | Retrieval failure: fix chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, filters, query rewriting |
| No | No | Retrieval failure plus the model filled the gap from memory: fix retrieval and enforce abstention |
| Yes | No | Generation failure: hallucination or misreading; tighten instructions, reorder context, stronger model |
| Yes | Yes, but wrong | Context contained conflicting or stale info, or the question was misunderstood: fix data freshness, add answer relevance checks |

## Agent evals
Agents add multiple steps, tools with side effects, and non-determinism compounded across steps. Grade on two levels.

**Outcome (end state) evals** check whether the task was achieved, ideally by inspecting the environment rather than reading the agent's final message. Did the ticket get created with the right fields? Does the repository's test suite pass after the patch? SWE-bench grades coding agents this way: apply the patch and run the project's tests. τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024) checks the final database state after a simulated customer conversation and introduced pass^k, the probability the agent succeeds on all k independent attempts, which exposes unreliability that a single-run pass rate hides.

**Trajectory evals** check how it got there:

- **Tool selection:** for a given step, did it call the right tool? Compare with an expected tool, or a set of acceptable tools.
- **Argument correctness:** valid against the schema (code check) and semantically right (the date range matches the request).
- **Order and dependencies:** for example, it must look up the order before issuing a refund.
- **Efficiency:** number of steps, tokens, cost, wall time; loops of repeated identical calls.
- **Safety:** no write or destructive tool called without confirmation; no tools outside the allowed set; no data sent to unexpected destinations.
- **Recovery:** when a tool returns an error, does it adapt or retry blindly?

```python
def grade_trajectory(steps: list[dict], expected: dict) -> dict:
    calls = [s["tool"] for s in steps if s["type"] == "tool_call"]
    first_index = {t: calls.index(t) for t in set(calls)}
    order_ok = all(
        a in first_index and b in first_index and first_index[a] < first_index[b]
        for a, b in expected.get("must_precede", [])          # e.g. [("get_order", "issue_refund")]
    )
    forbidden = set(calls) & set(expected.get("forbidden_tools", []))
    repeats = sum(1 for a, b in zip(steps, steps[1:])
                  if a.get("tool") and a.get("tool") == b.get("tool") and a.get("args") == b.get("args"))
    return {
        "required_tools": set(expected["required_tools"]) <= set(calls),
        "order_ok": order_ok,
        "no_forbidden": not forbidden,
        "within_budget": len(calls) <= expected.get("max_calls", 10),
        "no_loops": repeats == 0,
    }
```

Do not over-constrain trajectories. Several paths can be valid; Anthropic's *Building effective agents* advises starting simple and measuring outcomes. Grade the outcome strictly and the trajectory on invariants (safety, required ordering, budgets) rather than one exact sequence.

**Simulated users and sandboxes.** Multi-turn agents need an environment: a sandboxed copy of the tools (fake payment API, test database, browser in a container) and often a simulated user played by another LLM with a hidden goal. Reset state between trials and run each task several times.

## Trade-offs
- **Component metrics need labels** (relevant doc ids, expected tools) that cost time to produce; end-to-end judges need fewer labels but explain less.
- **LLM-based faithfulness scores are approximations.** Calibrate them on a human-labelled sample like any judge.
- **Agent evals are slow and expensive:** long trajectories, several trials each. Keep a small, fast subset for pull requests and the full suite nightly.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Reporting only end-to-end accuracy, so every regression becomes a long investigation.
- Measuring recall@5 when the generator sees 10 chunks, or using a different k from production.
- Labelling relevance only from the current retriever's results, which hides documents it never finds. Pool candidates from several retrievers.
- Grading agents by their final message ("I've booked your flight") instead of checking the booking exists.
- Single-trial agent evals: a 70% pass rate can mean every task passes 70% of the time or some tasks never pass. Report per-task success across trials.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you can decompose a pipeline into measurable stages and know the standard retrieval metrics precisely, and whether you understand outcome versus trajectory grading for agents.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. Score retrieval and generation separately; keep an end-to-end score too.
2. Retrieval: recall@k for candidates, MRR or nDCG after reranking, with labelled relevant ids.
3. Generation: faithfulness to retrieved context, answer relevance, citation accuracy, abstention on unanswerable questions.
4. Agents: outcome checks against environment state, plus trajectory invariants (right tools, valid args, ordering, budgets, safety), several trials per task, pass^k for reliability.
5. Use the diagnosis table to route each failure to retrieval or generation work.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- How would you get relevance labels for 10,000 documents cheaply?
- Faithfulness is high but users say answers are wrong. What do you check?
- How do you evaluate an agent whose tools have real side effects?
keyPoints: Score retrieval and generation separately, and keep an end-to-end score as well
Recall@k says whether the answer was retrieved at all; MRR and nDCG say whether the best results are at the top
Faithfulness checks claims against retrieved context; answer relevance checks the question was addressed
Grade agents on end state in the environment plus trajectory invariants: right tools, valid args, order, budgets, safety
Run agent tasks several times; pass^k exposes unreliability that a single-run pass rate hides

check.why: Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result: 1/4 = 0.25. MRR averages this over questions.

A better generation prompt

check.why: If the right chunk is missing from the candidates nearly half the time, no reranker or prompt downstream can recover it.

options: Check the final message says the booking succeeded
Count the tool calls

Inspect the sandboxed environment to confirm the booking exists with the right details

lessons.title: LLM tracing and production monitoring
lessons.summary: Tracing LLM apps with spans for model calls, retrieval and tools; online metrics for reliability, latency, cost and quality; drift; and the feedback loop into evals.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Offline evals tell you whether a change is safe to ship. They cannot tell you what real users are doing today, which inputs you never imagined, or that a provider quietly changed behaviour on Tuesday. **LLM observability** is the production half of the loop: record what happened on every request in enough detail to debug it, aggregate it into metrics you can alert on, and feed the interesting cases back into your eval datasets.

Classic APM tells you a request took 4 seconds. LLM tracing tells you it took 4 seconds because the agent made three retrieval calls, the second returned nothing relevant, the model then called a search tool with a malformed date, and the final generation used 6,200 input tokens on prompt version 14.

## Traces and spans for LLM apps
The model is the same one distributed tracing has used for years (OpenTelemetry's trace and span concepts): a **trace** is one end-to-end request; **spans** are timed operations inside it, nested as a tree.

```text
trace: support-chat  (user_id_hash=9f2c, session=s_81, prompt_version=support@14)   3.9 s
 |- span: input-guardrail            42 ms   verdict=allow
 |- span: query-rewrite (llm)       380 ms   model=small  in=410 out=28 tokens
 |- span: retrieve                  210 ms   k=50  index=docs@2026-09-30
 |    |- span: vector-search        120 ms
 |    |- span: bm25-search           60 ms
 |- span: rerank                    160 ms   top=6
 |- span: generate (llm)          2,900 ms   model=large  in=6,200 out=410  cached_in=5,100
 |    |- span: tool:get_order        95 ms   status=ok
 |- span: output-guardrail           70 ms   verdict=allow
 '- event: user_feedback        thumbs_down  comment="wrong return window"
```

What to record on each kind of span:

- **LLM call:** model name and version, provider, parameters (temperature, max tokens), prompt template id and version, rendered messages (subject to privacy rules), output, finish reason, input/output/cached token counts, cost, latency, time to first token.
- **Retrieval:** query text, index or embedding model version, k, returned document ids and scores, filters applied.
- **Tool call:** tool name, arguments, result size or summary, status and error, latency.
- **Guardrails:** which check ran and its verdict.
- **Trace level:** session or conversation id, hashed user id, app version, feature flag or experiment arm, final outcome, user feedback.

The OpenTelemetry **semantic conventions for generative AI** standardise attribute names such as `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, and define spans for model calls and tool execution. They were still marked as in development at the time of writing, so pin the convention version you emit. Emitting OTel-compatible spans keeps you portable across backends.

```ts
import { trace, SpanStatusCode } from "@opentelemetry/api";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("support-bot");

export async function generateAnswer(prompt: RenderedPrompt, callModel: ModelCall) {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(`chat ${prompt.model}`, async (span) => {
    span.setAttributes({
      "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
      "gen_ai.request.model": prompt.model,
      "gen_ai.request.temperature": prompt.temperature,
      "app.prompt.id": prompt.templateId,
      "app.prompt.version": prompt.version,
    });
    try {
      const res = await callModel(prompt);
      span.setAttributes({
        "gen_ai.usage.input_tokens": res.usage.inputTokens,
        "gen_ai.usage.output_tokens": res.usage.outputTokens,
        "app.cost_usd": res.costUsd,
        "gen_ai.response.finish_reasons": [res.finishReason],
      });
      return res;
    } catch (err) {
      span.recordException(err as Error);
      span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
      throw err;
    } finally {
      span.end();
    }
  });
}
```

(`RenderedPrompt` and `ModelCall` stand for your own types.)

## Tools, described neutrally
You can build this on plain OpenTelemetry and a tracing backend, or use an LLM-specific platform that adds prompt and output views, datasets and evals on top of traces. Common options in 2026:

- **Langfuse:** open source and self-hostable; tracing, prompt management, datasets, evaluation scores and cost tracking.
- **Arize Phoenix:** open source; built on OpenTelemetry and the OpenInference conventions; tracing plus evaluation and dataset tooling, runs locally or hosted.
- **Braintrust:** a commercial platform centred on evals and experiments, with logging, datasets and prompt playgrounds.

Others exist (vendor-specific consoles, general APM products adding LLM views). Choose on: self-hosting and data residency needs, OpenTelemetry compatibility, how well it links traces to datasets and evals, and cost at your trace volume. Avoid deep lock-in by emitting standard spans.

## Online metrics
Aggregate traces into metrics you can chart and alert on. Group them in four families:

| Family | Examples | Typical alert |
|---|---|---|
| Reliability | error rate by provider, timeouts, 429s, fallback rate, parse failures of structured output | error rate above 2% for 10 minutes |
| Performance | p50/p95 latency per span, time to first token, tokens per second | p95 TTFT above budget |
| Cost | tokens and spend per request, per feature, per tenant; cache hit rate | daily spend 30% above 7-day average |
| Quality | thumbs-down rate, regeneration rate, escalation to human, no-answer rate, online judge pass rate on a sample, guardrail block rate | faithfulness pass rate on sampled traffic drops 5 points |

**Online evaluation** runs your graders on a sample of production traffic: cheap code checks on everything, LLM judges on a few percent (or on traces with negative feedback). These are the same graders you use offline, so offline and online numbers are comparable.

Implicit signals are often more honest than explicit ratings. Few users click thumbs; many copy the answer, rephrase and retry, abandon, or ask for a human. Define these as events and track them.

## Drift
Drift means the world changed under a system that did not. In LLM apps watch for:

- **Input drift:** new topics, languages, user segments or query lengths. Detect by clustering embeddings of incoming queries and comparing cluster shares week over week, or by tracking an intent classifier's distribution.
- **Data drift in RAG:** documents updated, deleted or added without re-indexing; embedding model changed for new documents only.
- **Model drift:** a provider updates a model behind an alias, or you upgrade. Pin dated model versions where the provider offers them, and alert when the reported model string changes.
- **Quality drift:** online judge pass rate, feedback rate and escalation rate trending down.

Google's SRE book chapter on monitoring distributed systems still applies: alert on symptoms users feel (latency, errors, quality signals), keep dashboards for causes, and make every page actionable.

## The feedback loop
```text
production traces --> sample + filter (negative feedback, guardrail hits, low judge score, new clusters)
        |
        v
   review queue (domain expert reads, labels, writes critique)
        |
        +--> new eval cases (dataset v+1)  --> CI regression suite
        +--> new failure category          --> new grader
        '--> bug ticket                    --> fix, verified by the new case
```

This is what makes evals compound over time. The review queue should be small and prioritised: 20 well-chosen traces a day read by someone who knows the domain beats dashboards nobody looks at.

## Privacy and cost of observability
- Prompts and outputs contain personal data. Redact identifiers before storage where you can, restrict access, set retention limits, and honour deletion requests. Do not log secrets or full documents when ids suffice.
- Full-fidelity traces of long contexts are large. Sample bodies (keep metadata for 100%, full text for a percentage plus all errors and negative feedback).
- Log asynchronously so tracing never adds latency or takes the request down if the backend is slow.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Logging only the final prompt and answer, not retrieval results and tool calls, so you cannot tell where a failure started.
- No prompt version on the trace: you cannot correlate a quality drop with a deploy.
- Alerting on average latency instead of p95 and time to first token.
- Collecting thumbs-down events that nobody reviews.
- Logging raw user content into general application logs with long retention.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you know what to capture per request, can structure it as spans, can name metrics beyond latency, and understand how production data flows back into evals.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. One trace per request, spans for guardrails, rewrite, retrieval, rerank, each LLM call and each tool call.
2. Per LLM span: model version, prompt version, params, tokens including cached, cost, latency, TTFT, finish reason; per retrieval span: doc ids and scores.
3. Metrics in four families: reliability, performance, cost, quality (feedback, escalations, online judge pass rate).
4. Drift: cluster incoming queries, pin model versions, monitor quality trends.
5. Sample failures into a review queue that produces new eval cases; redact personal data and sample bodies.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- How do you monitor quality when only 1% of users give feedback?
- Which spans would you add for a multi-agent system?
- How would you keep trace storage costs under control?

Record model and prompt versions, tokens including cached, cost, latency, TTFT and finish reason on every model span

Watch input, data, model and quality drift; pin dated model versions and alert when the reported model changes
Route negative feedback and low scores into a review queue that produces new eval cases

The server's hostname

options: Store full prompts in general application logs forever
Disable tracing entirely
Redact identifiers, restrict access, set retention limits and sample full bodies while keeping metadata
Encrypt only the model name
check.why: Traces contain personal data. Redaction, access control, retention and body sampling keep debugging value while reducing exposure.

lessons.title: Prompt versioning, regression suites in CI and model upgrades
lessons.summary: Treating prompts and models as release artifacts: versioned prompts, CI regression gates against a baseline, shadow and A/B rollouts, and safe model upgrades.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A prompt is code. It changes behaviour, it has bugs, it interacts with the model version and the retrieval pipeline, and it needs review, testing, versioning and rollback. Teams that keep prompts as string literals edited in place, or worse as text in a dashboard nobody reviews, cannot answer basic questions: what changed, when, why, and did it make things better?

**LLMOps for prompts** means three things: manage prompts as versioned artifacts, gate every change with a regression suite, and roll changes out to real users carefully (A/B tests, canaries) with the ability to roll back. The same discipline applies to model upgrades, which are the largest "prompt change" you will ever make.

## What a versioned prompt contains
A prompt artifact is more than the template text. Everything that changes the output belongs in it.

```yaml
# prompts/support-answer.yaml
id: support-answer
version: 14
model: provider/large-model-2026-06-01   # pinned, dated version where offered
params:
  temperature: 0.2
  max_tokens: 600
response_format: support_answer_v3          # JSON schema name
template: |
  You are the support assistant for Acme Shoes.
  Answer only from the sources below. If they do not cover the question, say so.
  Cite sources as [S1], [S2].

  Sources:
  {{sources}}

  Customer:
  {{question}}
variables: [sources, question]
eval_suite: evals/support/v7
changelog: "v14: require abstention when sources are empty (fixes 9 cases in v7)"
```

## Where prompts live: code versus a registry
| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| In the repo (files next to code) | Reviewed in pull requests, versioned with the code that renders them, tested in CI, simple rollback by deploy | Non-engineers need git; changing a prompt needs a deploy |
| Prompt registry / management service (Langfuse, Braintrust, provider consoles, in-house table) | Domain experts can edit; change without redeploy; labels like `production` and `staging` | Another runtime dependency; changes can bypass code review and CI unless you enforce it; the deployed code and prompt can drift apart |

A common hybrid: experts iterate in a registry or playground, but promotion to `production` requires the eval suite to pass, and the application fetches a specific version or label with a cached, in-repo fallback so a registry outage does not take the feature down. Whatever you choose, **every trace records the prompt id and version**.

## Regression suites in CI
The regression suite is the eval set run automatically on every change to a prompt, model, retrieval config or tool definition.

```text
pull request changes prompts/support-answer.yaml
        |
        v
CI job:  1. fast deterministic checks (schema, template variables, length) on all cases
         2. run candidate and baseline on the PR subset (e.g. 150 cases x 3 trials)
         3. code graders + calibrated LLM judges
         4. paired comparison per case and per slice
         5. post a report on the PR: pass rates, deltas, new failures, cost and latency
        |
        v
merge allowed if: no guarded slice regresses beyond threshold, overall not worse,
                  cost and p95 latency within budget  (nightly: full suite)
```

A minimal gate script:

```python
import json, sys

THRESHOLDS = {"overall": -0.02, "slice": -0.05}   # allowed drop vs baseline
GUARDED = {"refunds", "safety", "non-english"}

def gate(baseline_path: str, candidate_path: str) -> int:
    base = json.load(open(baseline_path))
    cand = json.load(open(candidate_path))
    failures = []
    if cand["overall"] - base["overall"] < THRESHOLDS["overall"]:
        failures.append(f"overall {base['overall']:.3f} -> {cand['overall']:.3f}")
    for s in GUARDED:
        delta = cand["slices"][s] - base["slices"][s]
        if delta < THRESHOLDS["slice"]:
            failures.append(f"slice {s}: {delta:+.3f}")
    newly_failing = sorted(set(cand["failing_ids"]) - set(base["failing_ids"]))
    if cand["cost_per_case"] > 1.2 * base["cost_per_case"]:
        failures.append("cost per case up more than 20%")
    print(json.dumps({"failures": failures, "newly_failing": newly_failing[:20]}, indent=2))
    return 1 if failures else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(gate(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]))
```

Practical points:

- **Run the baseline in the same job**, or cache baseline results keyed by (prompt version, model, dataset version). Comparing against a number recorded months ago with a different judge is meaningless.
- **Use paired comparison.** For each case, did it go from pass to fail or fail to pass? Paired tests (such as McNemar's test on the flip counts) detect smaller changes than comparing two independent averages.
- **Show newly failing case ids** in the report so the reviewer can read them. Numbers start the conversation; reading outputs ends it.
- **Keep the PR suite fast** (minutes, not hours) with a representative subset; run the full set nightly and before releases.
- **Control cost:** cache model outputs by input and prompt hash when only graders changed.
- **Tools like promptfoo, OpenAI Evals, DeepEval or Inspect** provide configuration-driven runners and CI integration; a 200-line script is also fine.

## A/B tests and staged rollout
Offline evals cannot measure whether users are actually better served. For changes that pass the regression suite, roll out gradually:

1. **Shadow mode:** run the new version on live inputs without showing results; compare outputs with judges and check latency and cost. No user risk.
2. **Canary:** serve the new version to a small share (1-5%) and watch error rate, latency, guardrail hits and negative feedback.
3. **A/B test:** randomise by user (not by request, or a user sees inconsistent behaviour), choose one primary metric decided in advance (task completion, resolution without escalation, conversion) plus guardrail metrics (latency, cost, complaint rate), compute the sample size needed for the effect you care about, and run for full weekly cycles.
4. **Full rollout** with the old version kept deployable for instant rollback, ideally behind a flag.

Online metrics for LLM features are noisy and often delayed (did the support ticket reopen within 7 days?). Be explicit about which metric decides.

## Model upgrades
New models arrive constantly, and providers retire old ones on a schedule, so upgrading is not optional. Treat it like a migration:

1. **Pin dated model versions** where the provider offers them, so upgrades happen when you choose. Aliases that float to the newest snapshot change behaviour under you.
2. **Run the full eval suite** on the new model with the current prompts. Expect some prompts to need rework: newer models may follow instructions more literally, format differently, be more or less verbose, or handle tool calls differently.
3. **Compare per slice, cost and latency,** not only overall accuracy. A model that is better on average can be worse on your most valuable slice, or produce longer outputs that cost more.
4. **Re-calibrate LLM judges** if the judge model is changing too, before trusting any comparison. Change one of product model and judge model at a time.
5. **Check structured output and tool calling** with deterministic tests: schema validity, argument formats, refusals.
6. **Shadow, canary, then roll out,** with the old model available as a fallback until the retirement date.

## Trade-offs
- Strict gates slow iteration; loose gates let regressions through. Start with gates on guarded slices and newly failing cases, then tighten as the suite becomes trustworthy.
- Thresholds on small sets fire on noise. Use paired comparisons, several trials, and a human reviewer for borderline results.
- Registries empower domain experts but need the same review and test controls as code.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Editing the production prompt in a dashboard with no eval run and no record of the old version.
- Changing prompt and model in the same release, so nobody knows which caused the regression.
- Gating on one overall average that hides a collapse on a small but important slice.
- Randomising A/B tests per request for a conversational product.
- Forgetting tool descriptions and JSON schemas are part of the prompt; a renamed tool parameter is a behaviour change.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you treat prompts and models with real release engineering: versioning, CI gates, staged rollout, rollback, and whether you can reason about noise in eval results.

**Model 60-second answer outline:**
1. Prompts are versioned artifacts including model, params, schema and tool definitions; every trace logs the version.
2. Every change runs a regression suite in CI against a baseline: deterministic checks, calibrated judges, paired per-case comparison, per-slice thresholds, cost and latency budgets, newly failing cases shown on the PR.
3. Passing changes go through shadow, canary and an A/B test randomised per user with a pre-chosen primary metric.
4. Model upgrades are migrations: pinned versions, full suite, prompt rework, judge re-calibration, staged rollout, fallback kept.

**Follow-ups to expect:**
- Where would you store prompts so non-engineers can edit them safely?
- The new model scores 3 points higher overall but worse on refunds. Do you ship?
- How do you keep the CI eval job fast and affordable?
keyPoints: A prompt version includes template, model, params, schemas and tool definitions; every trace logs it
CI runs candidate and baseline together, compares per case and per slice, and shows newly failing cases on the PR
Gate on guarded slices, overall score, cost and p95 latency; keep the PR suite fast and run the full suite nightly
Roll out through shadow, canary and A/B tests randomised per user with a primary metric chosen in advance
Treat model upgrades as migrations: pinned versions, full suite, prompt rework, judge re-calibration, fallback kept
interview: How do you manage and version prompts in production?
How would you set up an LLM regression suite in CI?
How do you safely upgrade to a new model version?
How would you A/B test a prompt or model change?

check.q: Why compare candidate and baseline results per case rather than only comparing two averages?
options: Per-case comparison is required by CI tools
Averages cannot be computed for LLM outputs
It makes the job slower, which is safer
Paired comparison detects smaller real changes and shows exactly which cases flipped from pass to fail
check.why: Paired tests remove per-case difficulty from the noise, and the list of flipped cases is what a reviewer needs to read.

check.q: For a conversational assistant, how should an A/B test be randomised?
options: Per user, so each person sees consistent behaviour
Per request
Per token
By time of day
check.why: Per-request randomisation gives one user a mix of behaviours within a conversation, which confuses users and contaminates the metric.

check.q: What is the main risk of using a floating model alias in production?
options: Aliases are slower
The provider can move the alias to a new snapshot, changing behaviour without your evals running
Aliases cost more per token
Aliases do not support streaming
check.why: Pinning dated versions where offered means upgrades happen when you choose, after the eval suite has run.
